Read these three domains as one Rossmann-like α/β nucleotide-binding architecture that has diverged into different families and functions. They are not one functional family. SCOPe places NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains in class c (α/β), with fold c.2 and superfamily c.2.1 as the main shared region. Alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domains, CoA-binding domains and potassium-channel NAD-binding (RCK/KTN-type) domains all use a βαβ dinucleotide- or nucleotide-binding module, so a shared fold or superfamily-level relationship is reasonable. Their evolutionary strength is distant. Shared fold means a common structural scaffold, not shared chemistry or a shared catalytic mechanism. Superfamily-level similarity suggests common ancestry of the nucleotide-binding module but says little about the specific ligand or activity.

The functional divergence matters most for transfer. The alcohol-dehydrogenase C-terminal domain belongs to a catalytic dehydrogenase architecture with substrate and cofactor chemistry. CoA-binding domains bind the CoA adenine and pantetheine moiety in acyl-activating enzymes. Potassium-channel NAD-binding domains are regulatory ligand sensors that bind NAD(H) to gate a channel and have no catalytic role. Do not transfer enzyme activity, substrate specificity, or catalytic residues from one domain class to another based on the shared fold. Finding an NAD-binding Rossmann-like domain does not imply dehydrogenase activity.

Limits: template and representative choice must be made at the family level, not the fold level. Structural similarity alone cannot assign function. Confirming a function requires external evidence such as ligand-complex structures, enzyme activity assays, or mutagenesis. Also verify family placements against the specific SCOPe release in use, because classifications change between releases. I did not check any identifiers against a live database, so exact family IDs should be confirmed in that release.
